instructions: Rinse 1 1/2 cups of rice until the water runs mostly clear. Add it to a medium saucepan with 2 1/4 cups of water, bring it to a boil, then cover and turn the heat to low. Cook for 15 minutes, then take it off the heat and leave the lid on.
Cut the cabbage into thin strips, about 1/4 inch wide. That should be about 8 cups. Cut the pork into 1-inch pieces and thinly slice the scallions.

In a small bowl, stir the cornstarch with 4 tbsp of water until smooth and runny, with no lumps left at the bottom. Beat the eggs in a large bowl with a pinch of salt, then stir in the cornstarch mixture.
Heat 1 tbsp of the oil in a 12-inch nonstick skillet over medium-high. Add the pork and cook for 3 minutes, until it's no longer pink and browned in spots.
Add the cabbage and cook for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring often, until it has shrunk by about half.
Add the dashi powder, mirin and soy sauce. Cook for 1 minute, until the liquid is gone. Taste it. If it's flat, add a pinch more salt. Transfer the filling to a bowl and wipe out the pan.

Heat 1 tbsp of the oil in the same pan over medium-low. Pour in half of the egg mixture. When the edges start to set, gently stir the middle for about 20 seconds, then stop while the top is still a little wet.
Spoon half of the filling in a band down the middle. Fold both sides of the egg over it, then slide the omelette onto a plate, seam side down.
Wipe the pan, heat the last 1 tbsp of oil over medium-low, and make the second omelette in the same way with the rest of the egg and filling.
Drizzle the tonkatsu sauce over both omelettes in a thin zig-zag, then do the same with the mayonnaise. Sprinkle the scallions over the top.
Cut each omelette in half and serve with the rice.
method_notes: RecipeTin Eats is the lead (a fallback, since it has only 4 ratings): pork and cabbage stir-fried with dashi, mirin and soy, folded into a thin cornstarch-set omelette and topped with tonkatsu sauce and mayo. Okonomi Kitchen and Kikkoman agree on the plan; Okonomi Kitchen uses okonomiyaki sauce and extra toppings, and Kikkoman uses only soy sauce for the filling. The omelette here is made with water, not milk, to stay dairy-free, and the amounts are scaled from 2 servings to 4 as two large omelettes in a 12-inch pan.
